17	## Description
18	
19	Essay writing is an important method to evaluate student learning and performance. It is also time-consuming for educators to grade by hand. Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) systems can score essays to supplement an educator’s other efforts. AWEs also allow students to receive regular and timely feedback on their writing. However, due to their costs, many advancements in the field are not widely available to students and educators. Open-source solutions to assess student writing are needed to reach every community with these important educational tools.

The first Automated Essay Scoring competition scored student-written short-answer responses, however, this is a writing task not often used in the classroom. To improve upon earlier efforts, a more expansive dataset that includes high-quality, realistic classroom writing samples was required. Can you help produce an open-source essay scoring algorithm that improves upon the original [Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/asap-aes/overview) competition hosted in 2012?
24	
25	Competition host Vanderbilt University is a private research university in Nashville, Tennessee. For this competition, Vanderbilt has partnered with The Learning Agency Lab, an Arizona-based independent nonprofit focused on developing the science of learning-based tools and programs for the social good.
26	
27	To ensure the results of this competition are widely available, winning solutions will be released as open source. More robust and accessible AWE options will help more students get the frequent feedback they need and provide educators with additional support, especially in underserved districts.
28

32

39	## Evaluation
40	
41	Submissions are scored based on the quadratic weighted kappa, which measures the agreement between two outcomes. This metric typically varies from 0 (random agreement) to 1 (complete agreement). In the event that there is less agreement than expected by chance, the metric may go below 0 .
42	
43	The quadratic weighted kappa is calculated as follows. First, an $N \times N$ histogram matrix $O$ is constructed, such that $O_{i, j}$ corresponds to the number of essay_id s $i$ (actual) that received a predicted value $j$. An $N-b y-N$ matrix of weights, $w$, is calculated based on the difference between actual and predicted values:
44	
45	$$
46	w_{i, j}=\frac{(i-j)^2}{(N-1)^2}
47	$$
48	
49	An $N$-by- $N$ histogram matrix of expected outcomes, $E$, is calculated assuming that there is no correlation between values.
50	
51	This is calculated as the outer product between the actual histogram vector of outcomes and the predicted histogram vector, normalized such that $E$ and $O$ have the same sum.
52	
53	From these three matrices, the quadratic weighted kappa is calculated as:
54	
55	$$
56	\kappa=1-\frac{\sum_{i, j} w_{i, j} O_{i, j}}{\sum_{i, j} w_{i, j} E_{i, j}}
57	$$

(source: MLE-bench `description.md`, github.com/openai/mle-bench)

# Overview

## Overview

The first [automated essay scoring competition](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/asap-aes/overview) to tackle automated grading of student-written essays was twelve years ago. How far have we come from this initial competition? With an updated dataset and light years of new ideas we hope to see if we can get to the latest in automated grading to provide a real impact to overtaxed teachers who continue to have challenges with providing timely feedback, especially in underserved communities.

The goal of this competition is to train a model to score student essays. Your efforts are needed to reduce the high expense and time required to hand grade these essays. Reliable automated techniques could allow essays to be introduced in testing, a key indicator of student learning that is currently commonly avoided due to the challenges in grading.

## Description

Essay writing is an important method to evaluate student learning and performance. It is also time-consuming for educators to grade by hand. Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) systems can score essays to supplement an educator’s other efforts. AWEs also allow students to receive regular and timely feedback on their writing. However, due to their costs, many advancements in the field are not widely available to students and educators. Open-source solutions to assess student writing are needed to reach every community with these important educational tools.

Previous efforts to develop open-source AWEs have been limited by small datasets that were not nationally diverse or focused on common essay formats. The first Automated Essay Scoring competition scored student-written short-answer responses, however, this is a writing task not often used in the classroom. To improve upon earlier efforts, a more expansive dataset that includes high-quality, realistic classroom writing samples was required. Further, to broaden the impact, the dataset should include samples across economic and location populations to mitigate the potential of algorithmic bias.

In this competition, you will work with the largest open-access writing dataset aligned to current standards for student-appropriate assessments. Can you help produce an open-source essay scoring algorithm that improves upon the original [Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/asap-aes/overview) competition hosted in 2012?

Competition host Vanderbilt University is a private research university in Nashville, Tennessee. For this competition, Vanderbilt has partnered with The Learning Agency Lab, an Arizona-based independent nonprofit focused on developing the science of learning-based tools and programs for the social good.

To ensure the results of this competition are widely available, winning solutions will be released as open source. More robust and accessible AWE options will help more students get the frequent feedback they need and provide educators with additional support, especially in underserved districts.

### Acknowledgments

Vanderbilt University and the Learning Agency Lab would like to thank the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Schmidt Futures, and Chan Zuckerberg Initiative for their support in making this work possible.

![BMGF_logo](https://storage.googleapis.com/kaggle-media/competitions/The%20Learning%20Agency/BMGF_logo_black_300dpi%20(1).jpg)

![Schmidt Futures Logo](https://storage.googleapis.com/kaggle-media/competitions/The%20Learning%20Agency/Schmidt%20Futures%20Logo.png)

![CZI Logo](https://storage.googleapis.com/kaggle-media/competitions/The%20Learning%20Agency/1200px-Chan_Zuckerberg_Initiative.svg.png)

## Evaluation

Submissions are scored based on the quadratic weighted kappa, which measures the agreement between two outcomes. This metric typically varies from 0 (random agreement) to 1 (complete agreement). In the event that there is less agreement than expected by chance, the metric may go below 0 .

The quadratic weighted kappa is calculated as follows. First, an $N \times N$ histogram matrix $O$ is constructed, such that $O_{i, j}$ corresponds to the number of essay_id s $i$ (actual) that received a predicted value $j$. An $N-b y-N$ matrix of weights, $w$, is calculated based on the difference between actual and predicted values:

$$
w_{i, j}=\frac{(i-j)^2}{(N-1)^2}
$$

An $N$-by- $N$ histogram matrix of expected outcomes, $E$, is calculated assuming that there is no correlation between values.

This is calculated as the outer product between the actual histogram vector of outcomes and the predicted histogram vector, normalized such that $E$ and $O$ have the same sum.

From these three matrices, the quadratic weighted kappa is calculated as:

$$
\kappa=1-\frac{\sum_{i, j} w_{i, j} O_{i, j}}{\sum_{i, j} w_{i, j} E_{i, j}}
$$

### Submission File

For each `essay_id` in the test set, you must predict the corresponding `score` (described on the [Data](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2/data) page). The file should contain a header and have the following format:

```
essay_id,score
000d118,3
000fe60,3
001ab80,4
...
```

- **April 2, 2024** - Start Date.
- **June 25, 2024** - Entry Deadline. You must accept the competition rules before this date in order to compete.
- **June 25, 2024** - Team Merger Deadline. This is the last day participants may join or merge teams.
- **July 2 2024** - Final Submission Deadline.

All deadlines are at 11:59 PM UTC on the corresponding day unless otherwise noted. The competition organizers reserve the right to update the contest timeline if they deem it necessary.

## Prizes

### Leaderboard Prizes

- 1st Place - $ 12,000
- 2nd Place - $ 8,000
- 3rd Place - $ 5,000

### Efficiency Prizes

- 1st Place - $ 12,000
- 2nd Place - $ 8,000

Please see [**Efficiency Prize Evaluation**](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2/overview/efficiency-prize-evaluation) for details on how the Efficiency Prize will be awarded. Winning a Leaderboard Prize does not preclude you from winning an Efficiency Prize.

## Code Requirements

### This is a Code Competition

Submissions to this competition must be made through Notebooks. In order for the "Submit" button to be active after a commit, the following conditions must be met:

- CPU Notebook <= 9 hours run-time
- GPU Notebook <= 9 hours run-time
- Internet access disabled
- Freely & publicly available external data is allowed, including pre-trained models
- Submission file must be named `submission.csv`

Please see the [Code Competition FAQ](https://www.kaggle.com/docs/competitions#notebooks-only-FAQ) for more information on how to submit. And review the [code debugging doc](https://www.kaggle.com/code-competition-debugging) if you are encountering submission errors.

## Efficiency Prize Evaluation

### Efficiency Prize

We are hosting a second track that focuses on model efficiency, because highly accurate models are often computationally heavy. Such models have a stronger carbon footprint and frequently prove difficult to utilize in real-world educational contexts. We hope to use these models to help educational organizations, which have limited computational capabilities.

For the Efficiency Prize, we will evaluate submissions on both runtime and predictive performance.

To be eligible for an Efficiency Prize, a submission:

- Must be among the submissions selected by a team for the Leaderboard Prize, or else among those submissions automatically selected under the conditions described in the [**My Submissions**](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2/submissions) tab.
- Must be ranked on the Private Leaderboard higher than the `sample_submission.csv` benchmark.
- Must not have a GPU enabled. **The Efficiency Prize is CPU Only.**

All submissions meeting these conditions will be considered for the Efficiency Prize. A submission may be eligible for both the Leaderboard Prize and the Efficiency Prize.

An Efficiency Prize will be awarded to eligible submissions according to how they are ranked by the following evaluation metric on the private test data. See the [**Prizes**](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2/overview/prizes) tab for the prize awarded to each rank. More details may be posted via discussion forum updates.

### Evaluation Metric

We compute a submission's **efficiency score** by:

$$
\text { Efficiency }=\frac{\text { Kappa }}{\text { Base }- \text { max Kappa }}+\frac{\text { RuntimeSeconds }}{32400}
$$

where Kappa is the submission's score on the [main competition metric](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2/overview/evaluation), BaseBase is the score of the "baseline" submission of the mean of each target on the training set, minKappaminKappa is the minimum Kappa of all submissions on the Private Leaderboard, and RuntimeSeconds is the number of seconds it takes for the submission to be evaluated. The objective is to minimize the efficiency score.

During the training period of the competition, you may see a leaderboard for the *public* test data in the following notebook, updated daily: [**Efficiency Leaderboard**](https://www.kaggle.com/code/inversion/automated-essay-scoring-2-0-efficiency-lb). After the competition ends, we will update this leaderboard with efficiency scores on the *private* data. During the training period, this leaderboard will show only the rank of each team, but not the complete score.

## Citation

Scott Crossley, Perpetual Baffour, Jules King, Lauryn Burleigh, Walter Reade, Maggie Demkin. (2024). Learning Agency Lab - Automated Essay Scoring 2.0. Kaggle. https://kaggle.com/competitions/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2

# Data

## Dataset Description

The competition dataset comprises about 24000 student-written argumentative essays. Each essay was scored on a scale of 1 to 6 ([Link to the Holistic Scoring Rubric](https://storage.googleapis.com/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/2733927/20538/Rubric_%20Holistic%20Essay%20Scoring.pdf)). Your goal is to predict the score an essay received from its text.

Please note that this is a [**Code Competition**](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2/overview/code-requirements).

# # Inference topics

# %%
%%writefile inference_topics.py
import os
import copy

import torch
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from datasets import Dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer, Trainer, TrainingArguments, EvalPrediction
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

train_df = pd.read_csv("/kaggle/input/learning-agency-lab-automated-essay-scoring-2/test.csv")

label2id = {
    'Car-free cities': 1,
    'Does the electoral college work?': 2,
    '"A Cowboy Who Rode the Waves"': 0,
    'Exploring Venus': 4,
    'Driverless cars': 3,
    'Facial action coding system': 5,
    'The Face on Mars': 6
}
id2label = dict(zip(label2id.values(), label2id.keys()))
print(label2id)

checkpoint = "/kaggle/input/predict-the-prompts/output/fold_0/checkpoint-405"

class ModelInit:
    def __init__(self, checkpoint, label2id, id2label):
        self.model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
            checkpoint, 
            num_labels=len(label2id),
            label2id=label2id,
            id2label=id2label,
        )
        self.state_dict = copy.deepcopy(self.model.state_dict())
        
    def __call__(self):
        self.model.load_state_dict(self.state_dict)
        return self.model


tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint)
model_init = ModelInit(checkpoint, label2id=label2id, id2label=id2label)

intersection_ds = Dataset.from_pandas(train_df)
intersection_ds = intersection_ds.map(lambda i: tokenizer(i["full_text"], max_length=1024, truncation=True), batched=True)

def compute_metrics(eval_pred: EvalPrediction) -> dict[str, float]:
    predictions = eval_pred.predictions
    y_true = eval_pred.label_ids
    y_pred = predictions.argmax(-1)
    acc = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    return {"acc": acc}

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="output",
    report_to="none",
    do_train=False,
    do_eval=False,
    evaluation_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=2,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=8,
    learning_rate=1e-5,
    lr_scheduler_type="constant",
    warmup_ratio=0.0,
    num_train_epochs=1,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    optim="adamw_torch",
    fp16=torch.cuda.is_available()
)

predictions = []

train_ds = None
eval_ds = intersection_ds
trainer = Trainer(
    args=args, 
    model_init=model_init,
    train_dataset=train_ds, 
    eval_dataset=eval_ds, 
    tokenizer=tokenizer, 
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics
)
# trainer.train()
# predict on difference dataset
test_preds = trainer.predict(eval_ds)
predictions.append(test_preds.predictions)
predictions = np.stack(predictions, axis=0).mean(axis=0)  # average the result of 2 folds

essay_id = intersection_ds["essay_id"]
prompt_name = [id2label[i] for i in predictions.argmax(-1)]  # convert prompt id back to prompt name
result_df = pd.DataFrame({"essay_id": essay_id, "prompt_name": prompt_name})
result_df.to_csv("topics.csv", index=False)

- **Improve the solution** `T`
  - decide: what can I change to improve my solution? → Improve the evidence for choosing changes | Repair incorrect or mismatched predictions | Change the information presented to the model | Change training examples or targets | Change the learned model | Change the prediction pool | Change prediction combination or output mapping | Make useful experiments feasible
  - desiderata · what fits this case?: The current predictions fail a schema, signal, or compatibility check. · The claimed gain is no larger than variation in prior unchanged runs. · Errors concentrate where the existing input representation loses available information. · A known noisy or shifted subgroup dominates the training errors. · Learning curves show underfitting, overfitting, or unstable optimization despite correct inputs. · Available candidate predictors make complementary held-out errors. · Valid cached predictions exist and output mapping or blending is not yet compared on held-out data. · Resource failures prevent the intended full pipeline or meaningful trials from completing.
  - **Improve the evidence for choosing changes** `T.1`
    - decide: Which uncertainty should I resolve before another performance change? → Choose a validation design | Choose a trustworthy comparison | Choose a response to an unsuccessful search
    - desiderata · what fits this case?: Related records, source shifts, or unstable target proportions undermine the present split. · Recent comparisons are confounded, noisy, or use a questionable metric. · Several recent trials failed to beat a reproducible baseline.
    - desiderata · added from expert visits: Marginal gains from the current line of changes have diminished to a small fraction of earlier improvements, suggesting saturation. · No working pipeline, validation scheme, or baseline model exists yet, so foundational infrastructure is the first uncertainty to resolve. · The pipeline cannot produce a valid submission due to runtime errors or missing components, blocking any performance comparison.
    - **Choose a validation design** `T.1.1`
      - decide: Which split design should I test for this data? → Preserve target proportions | Hold related examples together | Probe subgroup allocation | Change holdout allocation
      - desiderata · what fits this case?: Target classes or target bins are unevenly distributed across the current folds. · Multiple rows share an entity, source, or topic that should be unseen at evaluation. · A recognizable source subgroup differs from the evaluation population. · The proposed subgroup allocation places the same row in training and validation. · A large fixed holdout substantially reduces fitting data after model choices are settled.
      - desiderata · added from expert visits: The stratification variable used for fold assignment may not be appropriate for the target distribution (e.g., soft or noisy labels). · The grouping or clustering step for CV splitting receives incorrect input (non-feature columns, wrong data type, or mismatched features between fit and predict). · The number of CV folds is mismatched with the number of natural groups or the dataset size, affecting fold balance or estimate stability. · The target array passed to the stratified splitter is not in the expected discrete format (e.g., float instead of integer bins). · The column used for group assignment in the CV splitter does not correspond to the actual entity, topic, or source that should define groups. · The pipeline currently lacks any holdout or validation split, so there is no local scoring mechanism.
      - **Preserve target proportions** `T.1.1.1`
      - **Hold related examples together** `T.1.1.2`
      - **Probe subgroup allocation** `T.1.1.3`
      - **Change holdout allocation** `T.1.1.4`
    - **Choose a trustworthy comparison** `T.1.2`
      - decide: Which measurement would resolve the uncertainty in the apparent gain? → Measure repeat-run variability | Check local and external score agreement | Isolate one change | Align the evaluation callback | Inspect data structure
      - desiderata · what fits this case?: Unchanged runs vary by as much as the proposed improvement. · The public evaluation is tiny or disagrees with local model rankings. · The compared versions changed multiple independent settings. · Early stopping monitors a proxy, wrong dataset, or wrong metric direction. · The prediction unit or ordering of raw observations is not yet established.
      - **Measure repeat-run variability** `T.1.2.1`
      - **Check local and external score agreement** `T.1.2.2`
      - **Isolate one change** `T.1.2.3`
      - **Align the evaluation callback** `T.1.2.4`
      - **Inspect data structure** `T.1.2.5`
    - **Choose a response to an unsuccessful search** `T.1.3`
      - decide: Should I restore, narrow, or redirect the current experiment? → Restore the proven configuration | Move to a different improvement lever | Narrow the parameter search | Establish a working baseline | Test a coordinated bundle
      - desiderata · what fits this case?: A reproducible regression followed a change and the prior working configuration is available. · Several trials along the same lever show no reliable improvement. · Nearby tested parameter values bracket an improving region. · No complete pipeline has produced a valid measured prediction. · The candidate changes are coupled and a saved baseline permits later ablation.
      - **Restore the proven configuration** `T.1.3.1`
      - **Move to a different improvement lever** `T.1.3.2`
      - **Narrow the parameter search** `T.1.3.3`
      - **Establish a working baseline** `T.1.3.4`
      - **Test a coordinated bundle** `T.1.3.5`
  - **Repair incorrect or mismatched predictions** `T.2`
    - decide: Which failure mechanism should I investigate first? → Restore model and input compatibility | Locate a data-flow defect | Resolve the first execution failure
    - desiderata · what fits this case?: A new artifact or representation was introduced immediately before the failure. · Execution completes but outputs are constant, implausible, or omit configured components. · A traceback or absent output file identifies an execution dependency failure.
    - desiderata · added from expert visits: The model architecture definition does not match the structure expected by the checkpoint weights being loaded. · Inference-time hyperparameters (e.g., batch size) differ from training-time settings in a way that affects batch-dependent layers. · The ensemble blending weights do not reflect the known quality differences between component models. · The preprocessing applied during inference differs from what was used during training of the loaded checkpoint. · The config file shipped with new checkpoints contains default parameter values that differ from the actual training configuration. · The rank aggregation formula contains an arithmetic inconsistency (e.g., offset or scaling) that distorts the combined predictions.
    - **Restore model and input compatibility** `T.2.1`
      - decide: Which training-to-inference contract is broken? → Match architecture and weights | Match input preprocessing | Match tokenizer and vocabulary | Match feature schema and encoders
      - desiderata · what fits this case?: Checkpoint keys or tensor dimensions disagree with the reconstructed model. · Inference transforms differ from those recorded for the training checkpoint. · Vocabulary, special tokens, or token positions differ from training. · A downstream model receives different columns, encodings, or dimensions from those used in fitting.
      - desiderata · added from expert visits: Input file paths use a different ID format (e.g., float vs integer) than the files on disk, causing lookup failures. · The output activation or transformation (e.g., softmax vs log-softmax vs sigmoid) at inference differs from what the checkpoint was trained to produce. · The inference pipeline uses a different number of folds or ensemble members than the training setup that produced the checkpoint(s). · The inference script assumes a different training objective or output format (e.g., ordinal vs regression vs classification) than what the checkpoint was actually trained with. · The installed package or library version at inference differs from the version used to produce the checkpoint, causing incompatible layer definitions or serialization formats. · A variable in the preprocessing or inference code references the wrong or stale dataframe/array, so the intended fix or transform is not actually applied.
      - **Match architecture and weights** `T.2.1.1`
      - **Match input preprocessing** `T.2.1.2`
      - **Match tokenizer and vocabulary** `T.2.1.3`
      - **Match feature schema and encoders** `T.2.1.4`
    - **Locate a data-flow defect** `T.2.2`
      - decide: Where should I check for lost or corrupted signal? → Restore row and identifier alignment | Restore missing model contributions | Correct aggregation arithmetic | Trace inputs and prediction signal | Repair invalid numerical values | Correct the custom objective implementation
      - desiderata · what fits this case?: Data or predictions were sorted, concatenated, or joined without an explicit identifier mapping. · Configured model or fold counts exceed the number of accumulated predictions. · The blend magnitude or shape changes unexpectedly with member count. · Model or stage outputs are constant, placeholders, or derived from the wrong dataset. · Inputs, losses, or intermediate activations contain nonfinite values. · A custom objective edit preceded divergence or a catastrophic score loss.
      - **Restore row and identifier alignment** `T.2.2.1`
      - **Restore missing model contributions** `T.2.2.2`
      - **Correct aggregation arithmetic** `T.2.2.3`
      - **Trace inputs and prediction signal** `T.2.2.4`
      - **Repair invalid numerical values** `T.2.2.5`
      - **Correct the custom objective implementation** `T.2.2.6`
    - **Resolve the first execution failure** `T.2.3`
      - decide: What dependency failure prevents the intended computation? → Resolve artifact paths | Resolve package compatibility | Match computation devices | Repair syntax or API contracts | Write the intended submission
      - desiderata · what fits this case?: The error is a missing file or a read-only source path. · The failure is an import, missing symbol, or incompatible package version. · The error names an unsupported accelerator or mismatched tensor devices. · The first failure names an undefined variable, invalid keyword, type, or method. · The computation completes but the expected prediction file is absent or invalid.
      - **Resolve artifact paths** `T.2.3.1`
      - **Resolve package compatibility** `T.2.3.2`
      - **Match computation devices** `T.2.3.3`
      - **Repair syntax or API contracts** `T.2.3.4`
      - **Write the intended submission** `T.2.3.5`
  - **Change the information presented to the model** `T.3`
    - decide: Which input representation should I change next? → Represent repeated or structured records | Represent text for the model | Represent images and signals | Control the feature set
    - desiderata · what fits this case?: Examples contain repeated structured observations that the current features collapse inadequately. · Free text is the principal input and residuals vary with language or document structure. · Image or signal preprocessing discards potentially label-relevant detail. · An expanded or stale feature set is associated with worse validation or schema drift.
    - desiderata · added from expert visits: The expert is incrementally stepping through feature-selection ratios without a systematic sweep or recorded validation scores for each step. · The evaluation metric was recently changed, requiring re-evaluation of previously tuned representation choices under the new metric. · The ongoing feature-count or representation sweep has not yet peaked — the score is still improving at the last step tried. · Numeric precision (e.g., float16 storage) causes inconsistent representations of the same value across train and test splits. · An importance-based feature ranking is available and the current top-N cutoff has room to be tuned. · Engineered interaction features were computed at the wrong granularity (row-level vs. entity-level), so they do not represent the intended signal after aggregation. · The current preprocessing code has a runtime bug or library incompatibility that prevents it from executing correctly. · Preprocessing steps (scaling, imputation, outlier removal) were already disabled or simplified for the current model family, so re-enabling them is the relevant change. · A newly assembled multimodal or multi-checkpoint pipeline has not yet been scored on the leaderboard. · The pipeline uses overlapping or redundant input windows/segments and it is unclear whether all of them add signal. · Previously removed model components or checkpoints were dropped only for compute/resource constraints, not because they hurt performance. · The expert is already mid-sweep on a text vectorizer or representation parameter, making continued tuning of that parameter the natural next step. · The feature count was recently changed drastically and needs to be co-tuned with model hyperparameters. · A heavy NLP or preprocessing dependency is causing runtime or resource failures that block submission. · Cached predictions from a deep model are available but not yet included as features in the current model's input. · New feature columns are being appended to the feature list without re-running the feature selection procedure. · Domain-specific preprocessing that was part of the best-known configuration has been removed or is not currently active. · The current feature set lacks explicit domain-derived interaction or composite features that are known to be predictive. · The pipeline applies a single imputation or preprocessing strategy to all model families, but some models require different handling. · A rich encoder (e.g., BERT) already captures signals that explicit categorical features would duplicate, making those features redundant. · Categorical metadata is available in the data but not yet encoded as features for the current model.
